title: Contract Law Fundamentals
description: Core U.S. common-law contract concepts, from offer and acceptance to remedies for breach. For study only, not legal advice.
subject: law

cards.definition: A proposal to enter a bargain, made so the other party understands that their agreement will create a contract.
Agreement to the terms of an offer, in the manner the offer invites, which forms a contract.
Something of legal value that each party bargains for and gives in exchange, such as money, goods, services, or a promise.
Both parties' agreement to the same terms, usually shown through offer and acceptance; often called a meeting of the minds.
A response that changes the terms of an offer; it rejects the original offer and makes a new one.
Common-law rule that an acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly; otherwise it acts as a counteroffer.
Common-law rule that an acceptance is generally effective once it is sent, such as when mailed, rather than when it is received.
The offeror's withdrawal of an offer before it has been accepted.
A promise, supported by consideration, to keep an offer open for a set time, during which the offeror can't revoke it.
Legal ability to enter a binding contract; contracts made by minors, for example, are generally voidable by the minor.
Rule requiring certain contracts, such as those for an interest in land or that can't be performed within a year, to be in writing.
Doctrine that can enforce a promise lacking consideration when the other party reasonably relied on it to their detriment.
An agreement with no legal effect from the start, such as one for an illegal purpose.
A valid contract that one party has the right to cancel, such as one induced by fraud or duress.
Improper threats or pressure that force a person into a contract, which can make the contract voidable.
A contract or term so one-sided and unfair that a court may refuse to enforce it.
Rule limiting the use of earlier or side agreements to contradict the terms of a final written contract.
Failure, without a legal excuse, to perform a promise made in a contract.
A breach serious enough to defeat the contract's main purpose, letting the other party stop performing and sue for damages.
Money that puts the injured party in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed.
The injured party's duty to take reasonable steps to limit their losses after a breach.
An amount set in the contract in advance, enforceable if it's a reasonable estimate of likely harm rather than a penalty.
A court order requiring a party to carry out the contract, used when money damages are inadequate, as with unique property like land.
Part of the Uniform Commercial Code, adopted by nearly every U.S. state, that governs contracts for the sale of goods.
